finding: Second instance of the same repair pattern, in the other direction: §4 was made conditional this round and §1 still ships the unconditional promise. §1 deliverable 3: 'by_severity on tp audit --merge (§4) -- the breakdown that makes a blocking round's verdict readable. Emitted unconditionally, so it is the one part every project sees.' §4: 'Emitted when the round has at least one non-PASS row, and it survives --compact ... Emitting unconditionally would discard that signal and put the key on every merge of every default-all project, which is the case the twin excludes by name.' The two clauses give opposite answers on the input that decides the code: an all-PASS round. §1 is the paragraph a decomposer reads to size the release and to write the task; §4 is the paragraph that argues the design. Only one of them can be implemented, and §1's justification ('the one part every project sees') is itself falsified by §4's rule, since a project whose rounds are clean never sees the key.
suggestion: Rewrite §1 deliverable 3 to §4's rule: 'Emitted on any merge whose round carries a non-PASS row, and it survives --compact -- so every project sees it exactly when there is something to see.' Do not repair it the other way: §4's argument (the nonblocking_open precedent, taken whole) is the one this round accepted.

finding: §1 and §4 now give opposite answers to when `by_severity` is emitted, so test 13's word "Present" has no determinate meaning. §1 deliverable 3, unchanged this round: "Emitted unconditionally, so it is the one part every project sees." §4, rewritten this round: "**Emitted when the round has at least one non-`PASS` row, and it survives `--compact`**" -- and it argues the conditionality is load-bearing ("Emitting unconditionally would discard that signal and put the key on every merge of every default-`all` project, which is the case the twin excludes by name"). The two readings differ on an input every project produces: a merge of a round with zero non-`PASS` rows. One engineer asserts `by_severity: {}` is present; the other asserts the key is absent; both cite this spec. §1 is also where an implementer sizes the blast radius, and under §4 the claim that this is "the one part every project sees" is false -- a project whose rounds are clean never sees it.
suggestion: Reword §1's third deliverable to §4's decision in the same breath as the value: the breakdown a project sees on any round that carried non-`PASS` rows, absent when nothing was graded. Then §4 and §7 test 13 can be read together without a contradiction, and the "one part every project sees" claim goes with it.

finding: §1 deliverable 3 says by_severity is Emitted unconditionally, so it is the one part every project sees. §4 decides the opposite and argues for it at length: Emitted when the round has at least one non-PASS row, on the review twin grounds that its mere presence signals the state, and Emitting unconditionally would discard that signal and put the key on every merge of every default-all project, which is the case the twin excludes by name. So §1 asserts both the mechanism §4 rejects and the reader-facing consequence §4 rejects (every project sees it) as the reason the deliverable is worth listing. §1 was not touched in the round that rewrote §4, and §1 is the inventory a decomposer reads first.
suggestion: Restate §1 deliverable 3 from §4: emitted on tp audit --merge whenever the round holds at least one non-PASS row, and surviving --compact. Drop so it is the one part every project sees, or replace it with the true scope — every project whose merge round has a finding — since a default-all project with a clean round never sees the key.

finding: §1's deliverable 3 still reads "`by_severity` on `tp audit --merge` ... Emitted **unconditionally**, so it is the one part every project sees", while §4 -- rewritten this round -- makes the key conditional: "Emitted when the round has at least one non-`PASS` row". §1 was not touched by this round's repair, so the release's decomposition anchor and its mechanism section now specify two different emission contracts for the same key. This is not a cosmetic drift: §1 is the list a decomposer turns into tasks, and the two readings differ in the only property that costs bytes. Worse, no test in §7 discriminates them. Test 13 asks for `by_severity` "Present, correct over a mixed round, and still present under `--compact`" -- a mixed round has non-`PASS` rows by construction, so an implementation that reads §1 and emits unconditionally passes test 13, ships the key on every clean round of every default-`all` project, and reddens nothing. The one property this round changed is the one property the release cannot detect being wrong.
suggestion: Rewrite §1 item 3 to carry §4's condition, in §4's words, and drop "the one part every project sees" (which is now false under either reading you intend). Then add the discriminating input to test 13: a round with zero non-`PASS` rows must NOT carry `by_severity`. Every other test in §7 names the input that makes it fail; test 13 currently does not.

finding: The new value-scoped fence does not close the `tp import` deadlock for the users it was written for, and the paragraph contradicts itself doing it. §3 states both (a) "The fence is scoped to the *value*, not to a transition" — because "every route to `blocking` is a write of `blocking`" — and (b) "Value-scoped, an import that does not introduce `blocking` passes." *Introduce* is transition language, and by (a) it cannot be the test. Take (a) literally against §3's own premise that "`tp import` assigns the whole workflow block and carries the existing one forward when the imported document omits it": a project whose TASK-file override already holds `audit_converge_on: blocking` (set via `tp set --workflow`, which §3 lists as a write path, so the value lands in the task file rather than `.tp/config.json`) has every subsequent import write `blocking` as the carried-forward value. That import is refused, and Workflow A step 6 deadlocks under `tp run` for exactly the opt-in project this release exists for — the identical failure, on the identical path, that the round-8 repair claims to have removed. The repair narrowed the blast radius from all opt-in projects to those that set the field at the task layer; it did not remove it.
suggestion: Decide and state which of the two the fence tests, in one sentence, and price the case §3 currently leaves out. Either the fence is over the value being WRITTEN (then say plainly that a carry-forward import of an existing `blocking` is refused, and name the operator's route out — re-import under an operator, or set the field only at the project layer, where import never writes it), or the fence is over the RESOLVED value CHANGING to `blocking` (then delete "not to a transition" and answer the walk-around argument, e.g. by noting that a unit writing `all` then `blocking` is refused on the second write). Do not leave both sentences standing.

finding: The value scoping does not remove the tp import deadlock it was written to remove, and §3's own escape sentence silently switches to the transition scoping the paragraph above it rejects. §3 states the scope as the value written: 'blocking is refused on every write path'. It then justifies value scoping by the import case: 'a field-scoped fence would refuse EVERY import a project makes after it has once set the field -- deadlocking Workflow A step 6 under tp run ... Value-scoped, an import that does not INTRODUCE blocking passes.' Those are not the same predicate. tp import preserves the existing workflow when the imported document omits it (internal/cli/importcmd.go:154-161: '(§9.3): when the target exists and the imported document carries no top-level workflow key ... the existing file's workflow block is carried over', tf.Workflow = existing.Workflow). So for a project that has set blocking -- the only projects this release exists for -- every subsequent bare-array or workflow-less import WRITES blocking, and a fence on the value written refuses it. The deadlock survives, on exactly the same users, for exactly the same command. The only reading under which 'an import that does not introduce blocking passes' is true is a fence on the TRANSITION (old != blocking && new == blocking), which the preceding paragraph rules out by name: 'A transition-scoped fence -- refusing only all -> blocking -- is one a unit walks around.'
suggestion: Pick one and state it as the predicate, not as prose: (a) fence on the written value AND exempt a write whose resolved value is unchanged -- then say so, and note that the walk-around objection does not apply because a no-op write cannot end a phase; or (b) fence on the transition and answer the walk-around objection (a unit that clears the field and re-sets it performs a transition, so the transition fence catches both writes). Either way, §3 must say explicitly what a carry-forward import does, since that is the case the whole paragraph turns on, and §7 test 11 needs a fourth arm for it.

finding: §3 states the fence normatively as value-scoped (blocking is refused on every write path; all is not) and spends two paragraphs arguing that a field-scoped fence would refuse every tp import a project makes after it has once set the field, deadlocking Workflow A step 6 for exactly the opt-in users this release is for. §7 test 11 then pins the opposite: each of the three write paths exits 2 under TP_UNATTENDED=1 for BOTH all and blocking. Test 11 is the only executable statement of the fence in the release, so an implementation that satisfies it ships precisely the field-scoped fence §3 rejects, plus the import deadlock §3 names as the reason for choosing value scope. The two clauses landed in the same round and cannot both be built.
suggestion: Rewrite test 11 to match §3: for each of tp set --workflow, tp set --workflow --project and tp import, a write of blocking exits 2 under the fence and a write of all exits 0 under it. Add the import case explicitly (an import whose workflow block carries the already-set blocking value forward passes), since that is the deadlock §3 says the scoping exists to avoid and no test currently reaches it.

finding: §6a item 3 says the document that quotes engine.DivergenceHint verbatim is skills/tp/REFERENCE.md, which is what the docs-contract guard compares against — so this reversal and the one above are one edit. Measured against the guard it names, internal/cli/docs_contract_test.go, that is false in both directions. The guard holds the sentence in TWO independent ways: line 132 asserts the test-local literal divergenceCountingSubstring (audit convergence still counts every non-PASS row) against skills/tp/SKILL.md, and line 145 asserts the shipped engine.DivergenceHint against skills/tp/REFERENCE.md. SKILL.md carries the sentence as its own prose (SKILL.md:149), not as a quote of the constant, so editing the constant leaves SKILL.md untouched and the SKILL.md assertion green with a now-false sentence. Item 2 and item 3 are therefore at least three edits (the constant, REFERENCE.md verbatim copy, SKILL.md prose) plus the test literal, not one. §7 test 14 compounds it by naming SKILL.md where §6a item 3 names REFERENCE.md, and then justifying it with so the documentation cannot drift from the constant — a property that holds only for REFERENCE.md.
suggestion: Replace the one edit claim with the actual edit set and name each document once: engine.DivergenceHint, its verbatim copy in skills/tp/REFERENCE.md, the independent prose sentence in skills/tp/SKILL.md, and the test-local literal divergenceCountingSubstring that pins the SKILL.md half. State in test 14 that BOTH documents must state a rule true under both values, and keep the cannot-drift-from-the-constant claim attached only to REFERENCE.md.

finding: Test 11 is byte-identical to its round-8 text and still asserts the FIELD-scoped fence that §3 was rewritten this round to reject: "Each of `tp set --workflow`, `tp set --workflow --project` and `tp import` exits 2 under `TP_UNATTENDED=1` for both `all` and `blocking`, and 0 without it." §3 now decides the opposite — "`blocking` is refused on every write path; `all` is not" — and gives the reason (a field-scoped fence "costs a run-halting escalation for a write that cannot end a phase early" and deadlocks `tp import`). §7 is the list an implementer builds against, so the release ships the field-scoped fence and the `tp import` deadlock the round-8 repair was made to remove, with a green test suite proving it. This is the only place the reversed decision survives, which is what makes it dangerous: §3 reads correct while the executable contract reads the old rule.
suggestion: Rewrite test 11 to the value-scoped rule: each of the three write paths exits 2 under `TP_UNATTENDED=1` when the written value is `blocking`, and exits 0 under `TP_UNATTENDED=1` when the written value is `all` — the second half being the assertion that fails against a field-scoped implementation and is therefore the one that pins §3's decision. Keep the unset-`TP_UNATTENDED` case at 0 for both values, and keep one assertion per path.

finding: Test 11 mandates the exact fence §3 rejects, in the same release, so the two sections cannot both be satisfied. §3 decides value scoping this round and states it twice: "`blocking` is refused on every write path; `all` is not. The fence is scoped to the *value*, not to a transition and not to the field", and "A *field*-scoped fence is wider than the argument for it: `all` is the built-in default and the only value that tightens the gate, so refusing it buys nothing and costs a run-halting escalation". Test 11 still reads "Each of `tp set --workflow`, `tp set --workflow --project` and `tp import` exits 2 under `TP_UNATTENDED=1` for both `all` and `blocking`, and 0 without it" -- byte-identical to round 8's wording (verified against snapshot-round-8.md line 195 vs snapshot-round-9.md line 257). An implementation that satisfies test 11 is field-scoped and therefore violates §3; an implementation that satisfies §3 reddens test 11 on three of its six assertions. This is not merely an ambiguity: it is the one input on which the release's central decision this round turns, and §7 is where the implementer gets acceptance from.
suggestion: Rewrite test 11 to the value-scoped fence and keep the two-sinks discipline: under `TP_UNATTENDED=1`, each of the three write paths exits 2 for `blocking`; each of the three exits 0 for `all` and writes it; without `TP_UNATTENDED` all six exit 0. Name the killing mutation explicitly -- a fence keyed on the field name rather than on the value, which is the cheapest branch to add and passes today's wording.

finding: Test 11 mandates the field-scoped fence §3 spent this round removing. It reads: "Each of `tp set --workflow`, `tp set --workflow --project` and `tp import` exits 2 under `TP_UNATTENDED=1` **for both `all` and `blocking`**, and 0 without it." §3's decision is the opposite and is stated in bold: "**`blocking` is refused on every write path; `all` is not.** The fence is scoped to the *value*, not to a transition and not to the field." Between the two, the test wins -- it is what an implementer builds against and what a gate enforces -- so the release as written ships the field-scoped fence together with both costs §3 enumerates as its reason for not shipping it: a run-halting escalation for a write of `all`, which "cannot end a phase early", and the `tp import` deadlock, where "a field-scoped fence would refuse **every** import a project makes after it has once set the field -- deadlocking Workflow A step 6 under `tp run`, for exactly the opt-in users this release is for". The most expensive round-trip tp has, re-armed by a clause in §7 that the §3 repair did not reach.
suggestion: Test 11 should assert the scoping, not contradict it: under `TP_UNATTENDED=1`, each of the three write paths exits 2 for `blocking` and 0 for `all`, and 0 for `blocking` without the variable. That is three assertions per path with a real discriminating input -- an implementation with a field-scoped fence fails the `all` case, which the current wording is written to require. Add the import case explicitly: an import whose workflow block carries a pre-existing `blocking` value forward, without introducing it, must pass (§3's "an import that does not introduce `blocking` passes") -- otherwise the deadlock ships under a value-scoped fence too.

finding: This round's fence repair made §3 value-scoped and left §7 test 11 pinning the field-scoped reading it replaced, so the release's own acceptance criterion FAILS a correct implementation. §3: 'blocking is refused on every write path; all is not. The fence is scoped to the value, not to a transition and not to the field.' Test 11: 'Each of tp set --workflow, tp set --workflow --project and tp import exits 2 under TP_UNATTENDED=1 for both all and blocking, and 0 without it.' Under §3, `tp set --workflow audit_converge_on=all` under TP_UNATTENDED=1 must exit 0 (the value tightens the gate and refusing it 'buys nothing and costs a run-halting escalation for a write that cannot end a phase early'). Under test 11 it must exit 2. An implementer building §3 reddens test 11; an implementer building test 11 ships the field-scoped fence §3 spends a paragraph rejecting. There is no third reading: the two clauses are contradictory over one input the release names in both.
suggestion: Rewrite test 11 to the value scoping: each of the three paths exits 2 under TP_UNATTENDED=1 when the write's resolved value is `blocking`, and exits 0 under TP_UNATTENDED=1 when it is `all` -- the `all` case being the negative control that separates a value-scoped fence from a field-scoped one. Keep 'and 0 without it' as the third arm.

finding: §1 announces Three deliverables and enumerates them, and that list is what a decomposer reads to size the release. The document now contains at least two further pieces of work that declare themselves in scope and appear in no deliverable: §2 changes the next_action recommendation under blocking (the recommendation must name the accepted rows rather than report an empty round ... That is part of this release), and §6a asserts three shipped-assertion reversals with an explicit This is work, not a Non-Goal, added in this round because an earlier draft had hidden it in the Non-Goals list. Both carry their own tests (§7 tests 12 and 14). The header blockquote says this file is the decisions, so the inventory being short by two is not a survey detail — a decomposer building §1 literally omits the next_action branch and the three reversals.
suggestion: Either raise the count and add the two items to §1 (a next_action deliverable pointing at §2, and a reversals deliverable pointing at §6a), or replace Three deliverables with a pointer that cannot go stale — e.g. this release ships §2, §3, §4 and §6a, with the sections as the inventory rather than a restated count.

finding: §4's emission rule was reversed this round and §1 was not touched, so the two now state opposite normative rules for the same deliverable. §1 deliverable 3: "`by_severity` on `tp audit --merge` (§4) — the breakdown that makes a `blocking` round's verdict readable. Emitted unconditionally, so it is the one part every project sees." §4: "**Emitted when the round has at least one non-`PASS` row, and it survives `--compact`**", with the explicit reason that "Emitting unconditionally would discard that signal and put the key on every merge of every default-`all` project, which is the case the twin excludes by name." An implementer reading §1 ships the unconditional form §4 now argues against by name. The trailing clause is false twice over under §4: a default-`all` project that merges only clean rounds never sees the key at all, so it is no longer "the one part every project sees" — which was §1's whole argument for listing it as a separate deliverable.
suggestion: Rewrite §1 deliverable 3 to §4's rule and drop the reach claim it no longer supports, e.g.: "the breakdown that makes a `blocking` round's verdict readable. Emitted on any merge whose round holds a non-`PASS` row, `all` and `blocking` alike, and it survives `--compact` (§4)." Then re-check whether the deliverable's justification still stands on its own without "the one part every project sees".

finding: The next_action half of §2's blocking-governs-clean paragraph is declared in scope and never given a form, so it cannot be built. §2: 'Under blocking the first clean round of a streak that still holds warning/info rows changes branch, and the recommendation must name the accepted rows rather than report an empty round. That is part of this release.' 'Name the accepted rows' has no shape anywhere in the spec: not a count, not a list of role/item ids, not a sentence template, not a new key. The existing next_action is a single command string an agent executes; whether the naming goes into that string, into a sibling key, or into an advisory is undecided, and the three cost different code and different output-contract surface. §7 lists fourteen tests and none of them is about next_action, so the acceptance that would settle the form at task time does not exist either. The rest of the paragraph IS buildable -- the two derivation sites and their invariant comments are named as work -- which makes the gap sharper: an implementer can do half a task and has to invent the other half.
suggestion: State the emitted form. Minimal version that keeps the release small: on an audit round that is clean under blocking with a non-zero non-PASS count, next_action's text ends with the count and the by_severity buckets it accepted (the numbers §4 already computes), e.g. '... (accepted open: 2 warning, 1 info)'. Then add it to §7 as a test whose failing input is a blocking clean round with warning rows -- an implementation that emits the all-round wording passes every test now listed.

finding: §2.1 now states the precondition honestly -- "**The cells below are reachable only when the field resolves before round 1 is recorded**, which is the moment an operator has none of the evidence this table offers ... the decision is made at the start of a phase, on the previous cycle's numbers" -- and then the release owes that operator nothing at that moment. tp ships no surface that yields a past cycle's severity mix: `by_severity` (§4) is computed on `--merge` of the CURRENT round's role files, so it exists only after the decision window has closed, and it is not persisted into the recorded round, so the previous cycle's numbers are recoverable only by hand-counting `severity` across that cycle's `spec/.tp-review/<base>/audit-round-*.ndjson`. The release therefore forces a decision to a moment it does not instrument, and its one unconditional new output arrives one phase too late to feed the only decision it could feed. Everything §2.1's table contains -- the two rows, the 93%, the missing `error` column -- is exactly what the operator needs and is available only as prose inside a spec file that no tp command reads. Against the AX lens this inverts: the release spends bytes on a per-round breakdown that changes no branch under the default, and spends none on the one number that decides whether to leave the default.
suggestion: Answer the question the precondition raises, in §2.1, in one of two ways and say which. Cheapest, no new surface: state the recipe -- the operator reads the previous cycle's recorded audit rounds and counts `severity` over non-`PASS` rows -- and give the exact command, so the decision has a documented derivation instead of an implied one. If a surface is warranted, the honest one is not a new flag but making §4's breakdown reach the recorded round, so the next cycle's operator can read it back; price that against `by_severity`'s current merge-only placement rather than adding both. Either way §2.1 should say what an operator does at the start of a phase, since §2.1 is the section that tells them that is when to decide.

finding: §3 extends a closed enum whose members are enumerated verbatim in five shipped places, and neither §6a nor §7 names any of them -- while §6a claims the reversal set is closed at three and test 14 says 'The three reversals and nothing more.' §3: 'This release adds audit-converge-on to that enum, maps the field to it.' What that touches, none of it in the spec: internal/engine/escalation.go's five constants plus escalationDecisions plus three comments that say 'The five decisions', 'returns the five documented decisions' and 'reports whether decision is one of the five'; internal/cli/escalate.go's Long help, '--decision is one of skip-gate, raise-review-cap, raise-audit-cap, import-force or other'; skills/tp/REFERENCE.md:347, 'decision is one of skip-gate, raise-review-cap, raise-audit-cap, import-force, other'; skills/tp/SKILL.md:247 and :372, both enumerating the same five; and internal/cli/escalate_test.go's TestEscalateAcceptsTheFiveDecisions, whose name and five-element literal state the count. Two of those are user-facing documents and one is a shipped help string, and internal/cli/docs_contract_test.go pins NONE of the escalate wording (zero matches for 'escalat' in that file), so the drift is silent -- exactly the failure mode §6a item 3 exists to prevent for DivergenceHint. Sizing is affected too: this is a second doc-plus-constant edit the release does not count.
suggestion: Either add a fourth item to §6a naming the enum's documented enumerations as the thing that moves with the constant (and drop 'and nothing more' from test 14, or restate it as 'the reversals this section lists and no other assertion'), or state in §3 that the enum extension is one task whose acceptance is the enumeration sweep, and let §6a keep its count of three by scoping it to REVERSED assertions rather than to all shipped statements this release falsifies.

finding: §3 never says WHEN the refusal fires. Its normative sentence — blocking is refused on every write path — is unconditional as written, and §3 mentions no gate: TP_UNATTENDED appears nowhere in the section, and the only contextual hint is a unit stuck in an audit phase under tp run. Read alone, §3 refuses blocking from a human operator at a terminal too, which makes the field unreachable and contradicts §1 (opt-in and human-only) and §2.1 (an operator who sets it accepts that trade with the numbers in front of them). The condition exists in exactly one place in the release, §7 test 11 (exits 2 under TP_UNATTENDED=1 and 0 without it) — a test supplying a normative clause the spec omits, which is the inversion §7 exists to avoid.
suggestion: Add the trigger to §3 in the sentence that states the scope: blocking is refused on every write path WHEN TP_UNATTENDED=1 (the environment tp run sets on every child); all is never refused; and outside an unattended run both values write normally. That is one clause and it makes §3 self-contained rather than reconstructable only from a test.

finding: 'Unrecognised' names two different sets in two adjacent sections, and §4 cites §2's predicate as evidence for the narrower one. §2's gate rule: 'An unrecognised severity is treated as blocking' -- against 'Audit rows use error | warning | info', so §2's unrecognised set is EVERYTHING that is not one of those three, which includes a string outside the enum. §4's bucket rule: 'A severity that is a string outside the enum keys on that string. A severity that is JSON null, absent, or not a string at all keys on unrecognised -- one bucket, because §2's predicate treats all THREE identically'. §2's predicate does not treat three shapes identically; it treats four identically, and the fourth is the outside-enum string §4 gives its own bucket. So the justification sentence is false about the section it cites, and the word an implementer greps for resolves to different code in the two places: a `isBlocking` helper and a `bucketFor` helper that must NOT share a notion of unrecognised, though the spec's wording says they do. The consequence is readable in the output: `by_severity: {"warn": 3}` on a round that was blocked, with nothing in the payload saying the bucket blocked -- while the section's stated purpose is 'the point is that nothing hides'.
suggestion: Either rename §4's fail-closed bucket so it stops colliding (`unreadable` for null/absent/non-string) and keep §2's word for the gate, or keep the name and correct the justification to what is true: 'null, absent and non-string share one bucket because none of them can be echoed back as a key; an outside-enum string can, and is, though it blocks exactly as they do.' Then say in §4 which buckets blocked, since §2 makes every bucket except warning and info blocking.

finding: §4 says it takes the twin's grounds "whole rather than half" and in the same sentence drops two of the twin's three conditions. The shipped twin (internal/cli/review_record.go and review_status.go, the comment §4 is paraphrasing) emits `nonblocking_open` "solely when clean and that count is positive ... absent on a non-clean round, on a clean round with zero non-blocking survivors, and under `review_converge_on=all`", and the code is `if liveClean { if nbo := ...; nbo > 0 {`. Three conditions: clean, non-zero, and not-`all`. §4 keeps only the second: "Emitted when the round has at least one non-`PASS` row". The rationale §4 gives for the key -- "without it an agent reading `clean: true` cannot see what was suppressed" -- describes a round that is clean AND carries non-`PASS` rows, which under `all` is impossible. So the condition is wider than the argument that buys it, in the same shape as §3's fence before this round's repair. The exclusion §4 believes it has bought is close to vacuous: it claims the alternative "would ... put the key on every merge of every default-`all` project, which is the case the twin excludes by name", but under the chosen rule a default-`all` project still gets the key on every merge of every round that has any finding at all -- i.e. every round except the converging ones. The key is present exactly where it decides nothing (under `all`, `by_status`'s non-`PASS` total already determines the verdict, and the merged rows the same output carries already hold every severity) and absent exactly where its presence would have been the signal.
suggestion: Copy the twin's actual predicate: emit `by_severity` when the round is clean and carries at least one non-`PASS` row -- which is unreachable under `all` and is precisely the suppressed-rows case §4 exists for -- and delete the sentence claiming the current rule excludes default-`all` projects, because it does not. If `--merge` cannot see the round's `clean` verdict (it runs before `--record`), then say so and gate on the resolved `audit_converge_on` instead; either predicate is the twin's, and the current one is neither.

finding: Non-Goal 4 defers nonblocking_open on --record and --status, cites four places that pin its absence THERE by name, and clears exactly one thing: §4 --merge breakdown is a different surface and none of the four reaches it. But §2 also puts new severity-aware output on those same two sinks — under blocking the first clean round of a streak that still holds warning/info rows changes branch, and the recommendation must name the accepted rows rather than report an empty round. That is part of this release. next_action is emitted on --record and --status, so §2 ships a next_action string that names the non-blocking rows on precisely the two outputs Non-Goal 4 fences, and §6 clearing sentence never mentions it. Either the four pinned places reach it and the release reddens them, or they do not and §6 has not said so; and a recommendation naming the accepted rows on --record/--status conveys what nonblocking_open would convey there, under a different key.
suggestion: Extend §6 Non-Goal 4 to dispose of §2 next_action change explicitly — state whether any of the four pinned absences constrains the next_action string, and say why naming accepted rows inside next_action is not nonblocking_open under another name. If the answer is that it is, either move the next_action wording change out with it or lift the non-goal for that surface.

finding: §6a item 3 names the wrong document for reversal 2 and draws a false conclusion from it, in text that round 8's version had right. Round 8 said "the docs-contract guard pinning a **`SKILL.md`** sentence that says audit convergence counts every non-`PASS` row". §6a drops the document from item 2 ("pinned against a shipped document") and then item 3 supplies one: "The document that quotes it verbatim is `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md`, which is what the docs-contract guard compares against — so this reversal and the one above are one edit." Checked against the tree: `internal/cli/docs_contract_test.go:96` defines `divergenceCountingSubstring = "audit convergence still counts every non-PASS row"` and line 131-133 asserts it against `skills/tp/SKILL.md` only; REFERENCE.md is a separate assertion (line 145) of `engine.DivergenceHint` itself. So the two reversals touch two different documents and are not one edit — the release needs three coordinated edits (the constant, REFERENCE.md which quotes it verbatim, and SKILL.md's standalone literal). Item 2's added clause "so the document and the constant move together or the guard reddens" is false for SKILL.md's sentence, which is pinned as a bare literal and not against the constant at all. An implementer who believes "one edit" edits the constant and REFERENCE.md, leaves SKILL.md's now-false sentence shipped, and reddens the guard — which is the drift §6a exists to prevent. Test 14 ("both `SKILL.md` and `engine.DivergenceHint`") is the half that is correct; §6a is the half to fix.
suggestion: Restore the document to item 2 — "the docs-contract guard's pinned `skills/tp/SKILL.md` sentence" — and rewrite item 3's last clause to state the actual coupling: the constant is quoted verbatim in `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md`, so reversing it is an edit to the constant plus REFERENCE.md, and SKILL.md's separately pinned literal is a third edit that must land in the same change or the guard reddens.

finding: Test 14's repaired count is arithmetically right and still passes against the mutation it was repaired to catch. Counted against the tree: `TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate` (internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go:469-503) contains exactly eleven assert/require call sites, and exactly two of them -- `assert.NotEqual(t, 0, code, "audit_converge_on is not a workflow field")` and `assert.Contains(t, stdout+stderr, "unknown workflow field: audit_converge_on")` -- are the pair §6a reverses, so eleven, two and nine all verify. But "All **nine** surviving assertions of the gate guard still pass" is satisfied by DELETING lines 472-474 rather than flipping their expectations: the guard then holds nine assertions, all nine pass, and the file no longer exercises `audit_converge_on` anywhere. That is the same delete-instead-of-update hazard the draft anticipates for the seven-deletion case and does not close for the two-deletion case, and it is the cheaper of the two edits. Related and unstated: reversing the pair makes the `tp set --workflow --project audit_converge_on=blocking` at line 472 SUCCEED, so assertions 3-11 then execute with the project resolved to `blocking` -- they survive only because `signalRow` (audit_signal_test.go:40-42) emits no `severity` key and §2's fail-closed rule therefore keeps the disposed FAIL blocking at line 490. Nothing in §7 pins that precondition, so a later `severity` added to the fixture helper reddens the guard for a reason unrelated to this release.
suggestion: State the positive form: the gate guard still carries ELEVEN assertions, two of them with reversed expectations -- the `tp set --workflow --project audit_converge_on=blocking` write now exits 0 and its output does not contain "unknown workflow field" -- and the remaining nine pass unchanged. Add the fixture precondition as an assertion in the test rather than as prose: the disposed row carries no `severity`, so it is blocking under both values of the field.

finding: §2 added the symmetric-stamping paragraph this round and called the relaxing direction "the one to state"; test 9 still tests only the tightening direction, and a concrete implementation passes test 9 while violating the new paragraph. §2: "A round recorded under `blocking` keeps `clean: true` after the knob returns to `all`, so one operator-approved round of `blocking` relaxes that cycle's streak permanently." Test 9 records under `all`, switches to `blocking`, and asserts stored verdicts unchanged. The mutation that separates them is not the live re-grade test 9 already names but a policy FLOOR at the read side -- treat a stored `clean: true` round as unclean when the currently resolved policy is `all` and the round's stored `findings` is non-zero. That is the defensive thing an implementer reaches for ("do not trust a verdict recorded under a laxer policy"), it leaves test 9 green in both of its halves because `all` -> `blocking` only ever relaxes, and it makes §2's stated permanence false and §3's whole write-not-read fence argument moot. This is the half of round 8's repair that did not land: §2 gained the prose, §7 gained nothing.
suggestion: Add test 9's second half with its own killing mutation: record a round under `blocking` that carries `warning`/`info` rows and no `error`, set the field back to `all` without re-recording, and assert that round's `clean`, the cycle's `consecutive_clean` and `converged` are all unchanged on `--status` and on a `--record` of an unchanged results file. Name the mutation as a read-side policy floor, not the live re-grade, since the live re-grade is already named for the other direction.

finding: §2 gained a normative requirement this round — "Under `blocking` the first clean round of a streak that still holds `warning`/`info` rows changes branch, and the recommendation must name the accepted rows rather than report an empty round. That is part of this release." — and §7 gained no test for it. Tests 1-14 mention `next_action` nowhere. This is the clause that answers round 8's critical `derived-field-not-in-the-governs-list` finding, so the repair currently exists only as prose; §5 records the same shape as the reason the fourth deliverable was cut ("'prospective only' arrived as prose with nothing implementing it"). An implementation that leaves both audit sinks passing `!clean` into `engine.AuditNextAction` satisfies every test in §7 while shipping a recommendation to advance the phase with advisory rows unnamed — the invisibility §4 exists to fix, on the command §4's breakdown does not reach.
suggestion: Add a test naming the input: a round recorded under `blocking` whose only non-`PASS` rows are `warning`/`info`, asserting on both `--record` and `--status` that `next_action` takes the advance branch AND that its text names the accepted rows and their count. The mutation it must kill is the shipped one — deriving the branch from the non-`PASS` count instead of from `clean`, which is what the two invariant comments §2 cites currently assert.

finding: §2 states a required behaviour change to `next_action` on both audit sinks, says "That is part of this release", and §7 has no test for it -- nor does §1's deliverable list carry it. The clause: "Under `blocking` the first clean round of a streak that still holds `warning`/`info` rows changes branch, and the recommendation must name the accepted rows rather than report an empty round." Two defects for a test writer. (a) No observable is pinned: "must name the accepted rows" fixes no field, no key and no string, so one engineer asserts a count in `next_action.reason`, another asserts a new key, another asserts the existing command string is unchanged -- all three satisfy the sentence and only one can match an implementation. (b) No test in the list of fourteen mentions `next_action`, so an implementation that leaves both sinks exactly as they are today ships green: `clean: true` under `blocking` simply routes to the advance-the-phase branch and reports an empty round, which is the failure the clause names. `next_action` survives `--compact` and is the field the loop's driver branches on, so this is the release's most agent-visible behaviour change and its least tested.
suggestion: Either pin the observable and add a test -- a round clean under `blocking` with `warning`/`info` rows open emits `next_action` whose <named field> carries the non-blocking count, asserted on both `--record` and `--status`, killing mutation being today's code unchanged -- or move the clause to §6 as deferred. Do not leave a stated deliverable with neither a pinned observable nor an acceptance.

finding: §4 now names four input shapes for an ungraded severity and test 8 fixtures three, so the shape §4 added this round is the one the fail-closed predicate is never tested on. §4: "A severity that is JSON `null`, absent, or not a string at all keys on **`unrecognised`**" -- and it says why the fourth matters: "`\"\"` is not a bucket: it is what a naive type assertion produces for three different shapes, and it is the hiding this section exists to prevent." Test 8 still reads "three fixtures, for a severity outside the enum, `null`, and absent." The missing shape is the one where the naive Go implementation (`row["severity"].(string)`) and the correct one differ observably, and nothing rejects a non-string `severity` on the audit path. Measured: all 360 non-`PASS` rows in this repository's 90 recorded audit-round files carry a string severity (warning 158, info 109, low 36, error 26, high 16, medium 15), so the corpus supplies no instance of `null`, absent or non-string at all -- every one of test 8's fixtures has to be synthesised, and there is no reason to synthesise three rather than four.
suggestion: Make test 8 four fixtures: a severity outside the enum, JSON `null`, absent, and a non-string (`3` and/or `true`). Correct the trailing sentence at the same time: "A legacy row supplies only the first" is right, but it now reads as if the enumeration were complete at three.

finding: §4's conditional emission arrived this round and test 13 did not move with it, so nothing in §7 can fail against the rule §4 replaced. Test 13 reads "**`by_severity` on `--merge`.** Present, correct over a mixed round, and still present under `--compact`" — every clause of which an unconditionally-emitting implementation satisfies. §7's own preamble is the standard this breaks: "Each test names the input that makes it fail. Six earlier drafts of this list each contained a test that passed against unmodified tp." The input that discriminates — a round with no non-`PASS` row — is named nowhere. Same gap on the bucket rule §4 added in the same edit: nothing asserts that `null`, an absent key and a non-string all land in `unrecognised` rather than `""`, which §4 calls "the hiding this section exists to prevent".
suggestion: Extend test 13 with the two inputs that separate the shipped rule from its predecessor: an all-`PASS` round, where the key is absent from both the plain and the `--compact` merge; and a round mixing `error`, an out-of-enum string, `null`, an absent `severity` and a non-string `severity`, asserting the exact bucket set including a single `unrecognised` bucket of count 3 and no `""` key.

finding: §4's emission became conditional this round and test 13 did not follow, so the new rule has no test and its killing mutation survives. Test 13 reads in full: "**`by_severity` on `--merge`.** Present, correct over a mixed round, and still present under `--compact`." Every arm is a positive presence arm over a round that has non-`PASS` rows -- exactly the population §4's condition does not discriminate. The mutation that §4 exists to exclude, unconditional emission (an empty map on every merge of every default-`all` project), passes all three arms. Measured on this repository's audit corpus, 90 recorded round files hold 10,435 rows of which only 360 are non-`PASS`, so the majority of real merges are the case with no test.
suggestion: Add the absence arm and name its mutation: a `--merge` of a round whose rows are all `PASS` must emit no `by_severity` key at all (not `{}`, not `null`), and the killing mutation is assigning the counter outside the has-non-PASS-rows guard. Keep the two arms test 13 already has, and pin "correct over a mixed round" to an exact expected map rather than to the word correct.

finding: §7 opens with Each test names the input that makes it fail. Six earlier drafts of this list each contained a test that passed against unmodified tp. Test 13 breaks that contract for the decision §4 spent a paragraph making: it asserts by_severity is Present, correct over a mixed round, and still present under --compact — three properties an UNCONDITIONALLY emitted by_severity satisfies in full. The conditional emission is the whole of §4 disagreement with §1, and the case that discriminates it (a round whose rows are all PASS must carry no by_severity key) is asserted nowhere. Test 13 also does not pin the unrecognised bucket rule §4 states normatively, so an implementation keying null/absent/non-string on the empty string — the exact hiding §4 says the section exists to prevent — passes test 13.
suggestion: Split test 13 into three: (a) present and correct over a round mixing error, warning, info, a string outside the enum, and each of null, absent and non-string severity, all landing in the named buckets with unrecognised carrying exactly the last three; (b) ABSENT — key omitted, not an empty object — on an all-PASS round; (c) all of (a) surviving --compact. Name (b) as the assertion that kills the unconditional implementation.

finding: Round 8's architect finding of this class named two unenumerated consumers of `clean` and only one was taken. (a) `next_action` — taken, now stated. (b) the round entry's own stored `findings` count, which stays severity-blind, "so a stored round will read `clean: true` beside `findings: 4`" — still in neither of §2's two lists. §2's severity-blind list remains exactly the three it held in round 8 (`role_streaks[].open`, its `consecutive_clean`, `spec_coverage_clean_rounds`), and the reassuring sentence covers only the first of them: "Under `blocking` a round can record `clean: true` beside a non-zero `open`." A stored round entry carrying `clean: true` beside a non-zero `findings` is a second reconciliation an agent reading `state.json` has to make, and the section that just closed the identical gap for `next_action` still reads as a closed enumeration. Half a fix to a sticky class is how the class survives into round 10.
suggestion: Add the stored per-round `findings` count to §2's severity-blind list by name and extend the reassurance to it: `clean: true` beside a non-zero stored `findings` is expected and correct, for the same reason it is beside a non-zero `open`. If the list is meant to be exhaustive over consumers of `clean`, say so, so the next round can falsify it as a claim rather than infer it.

finding: The banner diagnoses a surface that grew with every repair and cut the repository survey; the file still carries a second survey of the same shape, of its own superseded drafts, and that one grew again this round. Nine passages narrate rounds 1-8 to a reader who was not there: the banner (lines 3-16, 14 lines); §1's "was in this release through five rounds"; §2's "An earlier draft wrote `all` as ..." paragraph and its closing note on why *surviving* is not the word (lines 53-58); §2's "Stated normatively because two earlier drafts left it to be inferred and both inferred it wrong"; §5's round-by-round account ("Rounds 3, 4 and 5 each falsified a different draft"); §6a's "an earlier draft left it inside the Non-Goals list ... The count is three because earlier drafts said one and then two"; §7's headnote "Six earlier drafts of this list each contained a test that passed against unmodified tp"; test 1's "six drafts never asserted it"; and test 14's "an earlier draft said two". Roughly 35 of 271 lines. The AX cost is not the disk: this file is re-read in full by every role every round (four roles times nine rounds so far) and again by the decomposer, and none of this text can become a task, an acceptance criterion, or an assertion -- it is unfalsifiable by construction, because the drafts it describes no longer exist. It also has no terminal condition: §6a's count sentence was added this round precisely because the previous round's number was wrong, which is the accretion the banner says it stopped.
suggestion: Keep only the archaeology that stops a specific re-proposal and turn each survivor into one clause attached to the decision it defends -- test 1's is the clearest earner, since it explains an assertion that would otherwise look redundant. Delete the score-keeping: the banner's finding counts, §6a's "the count is three because earlier drafts said one and then two", §7's headnote, and §2's closing note on the word *surviving*. If the history is worth keeping for the next reader, it belongs where the release already puts this kind of material -- the candidates file -- not in the document every role re-reads every round.

finding: The v0.36.0 row states two facts about a cycle that has not stopped: 13 rounds and never converged — no round reaches zero. spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/ holds audit-round-1..13 today and CLAUDE.md release table lists v0.36.0 as In flight, so a fourteenth round or a converging round falsifies both cells without anyone editing this file. §7 test 10 then freezes the same numbers into committed testdata (v0.36.0 thirteen recorded rounds ... blocking at 3 and all never), so the release ships a test whose expected values are a snapshot of a moving history, taken at an unspecified moment. This is the exact failure mode the header blockquote says the rewrite exists to end — a claim about the tree that the next round re-falsifies — surviving in the one place the blockquote says measurements may stay.
suggestion: Pin the measurement to what it actually is: v0.36.0 first thirteen recorded audit rounds, as of <commit sha>, none of which reaches zero non-PASS rows. Say in test 10 that the testdata is that frozen prefix and that the fixture is not refreshed when the live cycle advances, so a later v0.36.0 round cannot redden the test or silently invalidate this row.

finding: The `unrecognised` bucket introduced this round takes a word §2 already binds to a wider set, and the two extensions differ. §2: "**An unrecognised severity is treated as blocking.**" — which by §2's own predicate covers a string outside the enum as well as `null`, absent and non-string, since only `error`/`warning`/`info` are graded. §4: `error`, `warning` and `info` "key on themselves. A severity that is a string outside the enum keys on that string. A severity that is JSON `null`, absent, or not a string at all keys on **`unrecognised`**". So a row with `severity: "fatal"` is unrecognised under §2 and blocking, but appears under a `fatal` bucket, while the bucket literally named `unrecognised` holds only three of the four unrecognised shapes. A reader summing the blocking rows from a `by_severity` map — which is the map's stated purpose, "the breakdown that makes a `blocking` round's verdict readable" — cannot get it by reading `error` + `unrecognised`; they must know that every key outside the enum also blocks. §4's justification for the merge ("§2's predicate treats all three identically") is true of four things, not three.
suggestion: Either rename the bucket to what it actually holds (`ungraded_shape`, or `null`, keeping §4's argument that the three shapes must not be split) and state in §4 that every key outside `error|warning|info` — that bucket and any out-of-enum literal alike — is blocking under §2; or keep the name and say explicitly that `unrecognised` is one of several unrecognised buckets. One sentence in §4 tying the bucket set back to §2's predicate is what closes it.

finding: §4's two bucket rules give a real input contradictory answers. Rule: 'A severity that is a string outside the enum keys on that string.' Prohibition: '"" is not a bucket: it is what a naive type assertion produces for three different shapes, and it is the hiding this section exists to prevent.' A row carrying severity: "" -- a genuine JSON empty string, which a self-declared field an agent writes produces easily -- satisfies the rule and is forbidden by the prohibition, and the spec gives it no third home. The prohibition's own reasoning shows the two cases are distinguishable rather than identical: in Go, v, ok := row["severity"].(string) returns ok=false for null and absent and ok=true for a real "", so an implementation that keys on ok can tell them apart -- which is precisely what §4 asks for, and precisely what leaves the real "" with nowhere to go.
suggestion: Add one clause: a severity that is a string, including the empty string, keys on that string, and "" is a bucket only when it came from a real string -- null, absent and non-string values key on the fail-closed bucket instead. Or, simpler and one fewer case to test: fold a real "" into the fail-closed bucket explicitly, saying so, so the prohibition stops being a rule with a counter-example in the same paragraph.

finding: §4's two keying rules collide on one input and the collision is the hiding §4 exists to prevent. Rule one: "A severity that is a string outside the enum keys on that string." Rule two: "A severity that is JSON `null`, absent, or not a string at all keys on **`unrecognised`**." A row carrying the literal string `"unrecognised"` is outside the enum, so rule one keys it on `unrecognised` -- the same bucket rule two owns. The merged count is then unreadable in exactly the way §4 forbids ("Every row lands in a named bucket, because the point is that nothing hides"): an agent reading `{"unrecognised": 3}` cannot tell three ungraded rows from three rows an auditor deliberately labelled `unrecognised`, and the two have different remedies. Measured, the corpus supplies no instance -- the 360 non-`PASS` rows across 90 recorded audit-round files carry only warning/info/low/error/high/medium -- so like the non-string case this will first appear in the field, and test 13's fixture as described would not contain it either.
suggestion: Either pick a bucket name that cannot be a self-declared severity (a key no auditor would write, or a reserved form) and say so as the reason, or state the precedence explicitly -- a literal `"unrecognised"` string keys on itself and the ungraded bucket is named `<something else>` -- and add the colliding row to test 13's fixture so the choice is asserted rather than assumed.

finding: Test 10 is the largest artifact this release adds and §7 never prices it. "Each of v0.35.0's nine and v0.36.0's thirteen recorded rounds is re-recorded from committed testdata" -- measured on this tree, those 22 files are 3,046 rows and 1.4 MiB, and the repository has no `testdata` directory today, so this would be its first and would be a duplicate of bytes already committed under `spec/.tp-review/`. What it buys is a pin on a historical measurement (§2.1's four cells) that no code path consumes; the behaviour those cells summarise is already covered by tests 5-9 on the row predicate and by the streak arithmetic tp ships. What it costs beyond the bytes is a test that reddens whenever anything legitimately changes in a term it folds -- §7 itself names one, "`Converged` also folds a staleness term". Also unpriced: 80% of those bytes are `finding`/`suggestion`/`evidence` prose that no assertion in test 10 reads. The verdict predicate reads `status` and `severity`; restricted to `status`, `severity`, `role` and `item_id`, the same 3,046 rows are 295 KiB.
suggestion: State the size in §7 so decomposition can weigh it, and say whether both cycles are required: both rows produce `blocking` at round 3, so the second cycle's marginal information is the single "never converges" cell. Then say whether the fixture rows must be complete -- if `--record` accepts rows carrying only the fields the verdict reads, commit the reduced form and say so; if it does not, say which fields force the full row, because that is the reason a reader will otherwise assume was never checked.

finding: Test 10 says it reproduces §2.1 by re-recording each stored round, but omits the precondition §2.1 added this round and calls the honest shape of the offer: the cells are reachable only when the field resolves before round 1 is recorded, because clean is stamped at record time and setting the knob at round k converges no earlier than k plus audit_clean_rounds. A replay that resolves audit_converge_on anywhere after the first re-record produces different numbers, and the natural repair when the test fails is to adjust the expected values rather than the setup — which would silently re-falsify §2.1 rather than reproduce it.
suggestion: State the setup in test 10: the field is resolved before the first round is re-recorded, each of the two runs re-records the whole history under one fixed value, and audit_clean_rounds is 2. Add the negative half §2.1 already implies — a replay that sets blocking at round k converges no earlier than k plus 2 — since that is what pins the stamping rule against the live re-grade §2 rejects.

finding: Two findings formed and were dropped this round, recorded per the round instruction. (1) I was about to file that §2's record-time stamp does not record the policy that produced it -- a round stamped `clean: true` under `blocking` is indistinguishable in stored history from one clean under `all`, so an operator auditing a converged cycle cannot see whether the gate was relaxed, and §4's breakdown is on `--merge`, which is not persisted. Killed by my own lens before writing it: it is derivable at read time with no new byte, because a stored round that is `clean: true` while holding a non-`PASS` row can only have been stamped under `blocking`, and a round with no non-`PASS` rows is clean under both. No new field is warranted; if the spec wants the property, one sentence in §2 saying the policy is recoverable from the row set is the whole fix. (2) I was about to file §4's `unrecognised` bucket as duplicating §2's fail-closed predicate. Killed: the bucket names the same population the predicate blocks on, which is the point -- a differently-named bucket would be the drift, and §4 says so.
suggestion: No action for (1) beyond, optionally, one sentence in §2 stating that a round's governing policy is recoverable from its rows rather than stored. No action for (2).

finding: The precondition paragraph says The cells below are reachable only when the field resolves before round 1 is recorded, but the table it qualifies is ABOVE it (table at lines 101-104, paragraph at 109-114). There is nothing below the paragraph except a second qualifier and the missing-column argument, so a reader following the pointer either finds nothing or attaches the precondition to the wrong claim — and the sentence is the load-bearing honesty clause of the section.
suggestion: Change to The cells above, or move the two qualifiers directly under the table and before the missing-column paragraph so the pointer is unnecessary.

finding: The two conditions added to §2.1 this round point the reader the wrong way. "**The cells below are reachable only when the field resolves before round 1 is recorded**" and "Second, the cells assume `audit_clean_rounds: 2`" both refer to the four-cell convergence table, which sits ABOVE both sentences (immediately under the heading). Nothing follows them but §3. A reader who scrolls down for the cells finds the fence.
suggestion: Change "the cells below" to "the cells above" (or "the table's cells"), and make the second condition's referent explicit for the same reason.

(1) I was about to report §6a as under-counting the reversal by omitting README.md, on the strength of spec/0.33.0.tasks.json acceptance text saying README.md and skills/tp/SKILL.md each contain the substring. (2) I was about to report spec/0.46.0.md §8.4 (cited by §1 and §5) and §8.1/§8.2/§8.3 (cited by §6) as broken cross-references, after a heading regex returned zero matches against that file. finding: Fifth answer to the decomposability question, and the first with the import list attached. Verdict: THIRTEEN tasks, of which eleven are writable now, one is partially blocked and one cannot be written at all. Readable from the spec alone (five): audit-converge-on-field, audit-clean-predicate, audit-clean-stamped-at-record, audit-converge-replay-test, and audit-merge-by-severity modulo its two open defects. Need the tree, and their acceptances say so rather than restating a survey (seven): audit-converge-on-validation (the spec gives 'the same terms as review_converge_on' and names no exit codes or commands, so the twin's two sinks are the derivation), audit-converge-on-config-surfaces, audit-converge-on-fence (three write paths, three code sites, one shipped fence to copy), audit-converge-on-escalation-name (five enumerations to sweep), reverse-gate-guard-assertions (which two of eleven), reverse-divergence-hint-and-doc (which sentence, which document), audit-converge-on-docs (which documents). finding: Test 14 is a single 90-word sentence carrying four separate obligations spliced with three em-dash clauses and an embedded correction of an earlier draft: the nine surviving gate-guard assertions still pass; the count is nine because eleven minus two; an earlier draft said two and why that was satisfiable by deleting seven; `SKILL.md` states a rule true under both values; `engine.DivergenceHint` does the same; and the whole is asserted against the docs-contract guard. A decomposer has to split this into acceptance criteria, and the split is not visible in the sentence -- the clause about what an earlier draft permitted is the longest one and is the only one that is not an obligation at all. Every other entry in §7 is one sentence, one input, one failure.
suggestion: Break test 14 into its obligations, one line each, in §7's established form (name the input that makes it fail). Move the "an earlier draft said two" explanation out of the test entirely -- the assertion that nine of eleven still pass already forbids the deletion it warns about, so the explanation defends nothing that the assertion does not.
